quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The board voted 9–0 last month to close the Leeds branch. Yet Ines still raises it at every meeting, hoping someone will change their mind. A colleague mutters that she's ____.
quests.hint: The decision has already been made and cannot be reversed.
quests.explanation: To 'beat a dead horse' is to keep pushing an issue that is already settled. It differs from 'spin your wheels', where effort produces no progress on an open problem.
quests.usageContext: Informal and slightly exasperated; typical in meetings when someone repeats a settled argument.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the pointless image of whipping a horse that can no longer move; recorded in English since the 1800s.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person still whipping a horse lying motionless on the ground.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: Marcus blamed the kitchen staff for the wrong orders, but the receipts showed that the mistakes were made at the front desk when the orders were entered. He was ____.
quests.hint: He is directing his suspicion at the wrong place.
quests.explanation: To 'bark up the wrong tree' is to pursue the wrong person, cause or approach. Here the blame is aimed at the wrong department.
quests.usageContext: Informal; common in investigations, arguments and problem-solving.
quests.idiomOrigin: From hunting, where dogs bark at the base of a tree the prey has already left; recorded in the 1800s.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a dog barking at the base of a tree while the squirrel escapes elsewhere.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: For three weeks, Priya had rewritten the same proposal introduction, changing words and moving sentences, yet it wasn't any closer to being finished. She was ____.
quests.hint: There's lots of effort but no forward movement.
quests.explanation: To 'spin your wheels' is to put in effort without making any progress, like a car stuck in mud.
quests.usageContext: Informal; used for busy but unproductive work.
quests.idiomOrigin: From vehicles whose wheels turn without gripping the ground.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a car stuck in mud, wheels spinning and throwing up dirt.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: The gym only installed the fire alarm after the kitchen fire had already destroyed the equipment. Critics said it was like ____.
quests.hint: The precaution arrived too late to matter.
quests.explanation: 'Closing the stable door after the horse has bolted' means taking a precaution when the damage is already done.
options: letting the cat out of the bag
putting all your eggs in one basket
closing the stable door after the horse has bolted
quests.usageContext: Critical and slightly ironic; used for late responses and failed prevention.
quests.idiomOrigin: A proverb recorded in English since the 1300s, from the literal image of securing a stable too late.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture someone locking a stable door as a horse gallops into the distance.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: Before the big presentation, Angela emailed the slides to her manager, brought a printed copy, saved a copy on a memory stick and checked the room's projector. She wanted to ____.
quests.hint: She wants to prevent every possible problem.
quests.explanation: To 'cover all your bases' is to prepare for every possibility so that nothing is missed.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; used in business, travel and planning.
quests.idiomOrigin: From baseball, where players must protect each base.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a fielder guarding every base on a diamond.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: The investor didn't want to commit fully to either technology, so he put money into both the electric and the hydrogen start-up. He was ____.
quests.hint: He spreads the risk between options.
quests.explanation: To 'hedge your bets' is to reduce risk by supporting more than one possible outcome.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; common in finance, politics and personal decisions.
quests.idiomOrigin: From gambling, where a bettor places bets on several outcomes.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a gambler placing chips on two different horses.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: Nobody chose which department would handle the complaints; the manager simply drew names from a hat, and Kat's name came out. It was ____.
quests.hint: It was decided by pure chance.
quests.explanation: 'The luck of the draw' means an outcome decided by chance rather than skill or choice.
quests.usageContext: Neutral, often accepting or philosophical.
quests.idiomOrigin: From card games and lotteries, where results depend on what is drawn.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a hand pulling a folded slip of paper from a hat.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that completes the situation.
quests.question: The firm's cash reserves were almost gone when, out of nowhere, a wealthy investor offered to buy it at a fair price. It was ____.
quests.hint: A fortunate event that arrived without effort.
quests.explanation: 'A stroke of luck' is a sudden piece of good fortune. It focuses on the event itself, not on the odds that had to be overcome.
quests.usageContext: Positive; used for unexpected good fortune.
quests.idiomOrigin: 'Stroke' means a single sudden event, as in a 'stroke of genius'; used in English since the 1700s.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a lightning bolt of gold striking an empty wallet.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: With no funding, no equipment and two broken legs in the team, the small college side still won the national title. They had won ____.
quests.hint: Success came despite huge obstacles.
quests.explanation: 'Against all odds' means despite serious difficulties or a very low chance of success. The emphasis is on the obstacles overcome.
quests.usageContext: Dramatic and inspiring; used in sport and film.
quests.idiomOrigin: From gambling and betting, where odds are the chances of winning.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a small figure climbing a mountain against a howling storm.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: Three straight sales records made the department complacent. When the competitor's new product came out, they had nothing new to offer. They'd been ____.
quests.hint: They relied on past success and stopped trying.
quests.explanation: To 'rest on your laurels' is to be satisfied with past achievements and stop making an effort.
quests.usageContext: Critical; used for organisations and individuals who stop improving.
quests.idiomOrigin: From ancient Greece and Rome, where victors wore laurel wreaths.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a champion asleep in an armchair wearing a laurel wreath.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that completes the situation.
quests.question: During the meeting, an intern presented the very idea the manager had spent weeks preparing to announce the next day. The manager felt the intern had ____.
quests.hint: The moment she was preparing for was taken by someone else.
quests.explanation: To 'steal someone's thunder' is to take the attention or credit for something that another person planned or deserved to announce.
quests.usageContext: Common in workplaces and families; mildly resentful.
quests.idiomOrigin: Often attributed to the dramatist John Dennis, who invented a thunder effect for a play that was later used in another production; the story is popular but not certain.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a speaker about to unveil an idea, only to hear someone else trigger the thunder sound first.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: The praised engineer made no mention of the technician who had solved the problem, so the director stepped in: 'Let's ____; Maria found the fault.'
quests.hint: He wants to recognise the correct person.
quests.explanation: To 'give credit where credit is due' is to acknowledge the person who really deserves the praise.
options: give credit where credit is due
quests.usageContext: Positive and polite; often used to correct or add recognition.
quests.idiomOrigin: Recorded in English since the 1500s; the ethical idea is simple fairness.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a manager handing a medal to the quiet person in the back row.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that completes the situation.
quests.question: After repeated meetings, Suki and the supplier reached a deal by settling on a price precisely between their two offers. They decided to ____.
quests.hint: They compromised on a number.
quests.explanation: To 'split the difference' is to settle on a compromise by dividing the gap between two positions, usually in price.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; common in negotiations.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the idea of dividing a difference equally between two parties.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture two hands pulling on a rope until the marker sits in the exact middle.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: The two departments hadn't been on speaking terms since the merger. The new director organised a dinner so they could rebuild their relationship. She wanted to ____.
quests.hint: The point is repairing damaged relationships.
quests.explanation: To 'mend fences' is to repair a damaged relationship after a quarrel.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and constructive; common in politics and work.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the practice of neighbours repairing boundary fences.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture two neighbours fixing the fence that separates their gardens.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The unions and management were far apart on wages, but both wanted the factory to stay open. They began looking for ____.
quests.hint: They want something they can both accept.
quests.explanation: 'Common ground' is an area of shared interest or agreement on which a solution can be built.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and constructive; used in negotiations.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of two people standing on the same piece of land.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture two people standing on the same patch of ground from opposite sides.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: He kept staring at the puzzle until, suddenly, the pattern became clear and he shouted 'Oh!' In that moment, ____.
quests.hint: He suddenly understood something.
quests.explanation: 'The penny dropped' means that someone suddenly understands something that they hadn't grasped before.
quests.usageContext: Informal; mostly British; used for sudden realisation.
quests.idiomOrigin: Probably from coin-operated machines in which a penny drops into place before they work.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a coin slowly tumbling into a slot before a machine whirrs to life.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: After the heart scare at forty, Pedro changed his diet and started exercising. He said it had been ____.
quests.hint: A shock made him face reality.
quests.explanation: 'A wake-up call' is an event that forces you to realise a problem and change.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and serious; used for health, finance and behaviour.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the literal hotel service of calling guests to wake them.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture an alarm clock ringing loudly beside a sleeping person.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: For years, Hana denied climate change. After spending a summer working with farmers in drought-hit areas, she completely changed her opinion. She had ____.
quests.hint: Her view changed after new experience.
quests.explanation: To 'see the light' is to suddenly understand or accept an idea, often after resisting it.
options: seen the writing on the wall
quests.usageContext: Neutral, sometimes religious in tone; used for changes of opinion.
quests.idiomOrigin: From religious conversion stories that involve seeing a divine light, as in Saul's conversion in the Bible.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person emerging from a dark tunnel into bright sunshine.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: While everyone else in the office waited for approval, Ben publicly supported the unpopular plan and put his reputation behind it. He ____.
quests.hint: He took a personal risk by backing something unsupported.
quests.explanation: To 'go out on a limb' is to take a risk by supporting an idea or position that others avoid.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; used for professional and personal risk-taking.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of climbing out on a branch that might break.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person edging along a thin branch high above the ground.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: The gambler won twice, then insisted on doubling the bet again, though his friends begged him to stop. He was ____.
quests.hint: He continues after success and risks losing everything.
quests.explanation: To 'push your luck' is to take a further risk after having been lucky. It suggests that continuing might lead to failure.
quests.usageContext: Informal; often a warning.
quests.idiomOrigin: From gambling, where a winning streak can end at any time.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a gambler pushing a tower of chips onto a roulette table.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: Leaving fireworks lit inside the shed with the petrol containers wasn't a clever idea. The kids were ____.
quests.hint: They were doing something likely to cause harm.
quests.explanation: To 'play with fire' is to do something dangerous or risky that may have serious consequences.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and warning; used for risky behaviour.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the literal danger of children playing with fire.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a child holding a match near a pile of dry hay.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: She agreed to everything the client asked, then criticised every design choice. Her team couldn't tell whether she was truly happy. She was ____.
quests.hint: Her attitude keeps changing.
quests.explanation: To 'blow hot and cold' is to keep changing your attitude or opinion about something.
quests.usageContext: Neutral; used for indecision and mixed signals.
quests.idiomOrigin: From a fable by Aesop, in which a man blows on his fingers to warm them and on his soup to cool it.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person blowing on their hands, then on their soup.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The manager couldn't decide whether to hire more staff or cancel the launch, and each week the team heard something different. The plan remained ____.
quests.hint: Nothing is settled yet.
quests.explanation: If something is 'up in the air', it hasn't been decided yet.
quests.usageContext: Neutral and common; used for plans and decisions.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of an object tossed upward that hasn't yet landed.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a ball spinning high above two players waiting to see where it lands.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: After the crash, the patient survived surgery, but the next 24 hours would decide everything. Doctors described it as ____.
quests.hint: It could go either way, dangerously.
quests.explanation: 'Touch and go' describes a situation that is risky, and where the outcome is uncertain.
quests.usageContext: Serious tone; used for illness, emergencies and narrow chances.
quests.idiomOrigin: From sailing, where a ship might touch the bottom and then continue.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a small boat scraping the rocks and just floating on.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: With the final votes still being counted and both candidates within a whisker of each other, the result was ____.
quests.hint: Both outcomes are still possible.
quests.explanation: To 'hang in the balance' is to be in a state where the outcome is uncertain and could go either way.
quests.usageContext: Serious and dramatic; used in politics and news.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of scales balanced evenly.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a set of scales trembling in equilibrium.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: Ellis had no interest in the case; he just did each task exactly as instructed, without ideas or enthusiasm, and left at five. He was simply ____.
quests.hint: He is performing without commitment.
quests.explanation: To 'go through the motions' is to do something without real interest or effort.
quests.usageContext: Critical; used for people who are present but not engaged.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of copying the movements of an activity without feeling.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a robot mechanically stamping papers with a blank expression.

quests.instruction: Which idiom matches what is happening?
quests.question: The consultant's report was identical to last year's, with only the dates changed. Everyone could tell she had ____.
quests.hint: She did the minimum and didn't care.
quests.explanation: To 'phone it in' is to perform a task with minimal effort and interest.
quests.usageContext: Informal and critical; common in criticism of performances and work.
quests.idiomOrigin: American slang from the late 20th century, from performing without being present, as if by phone.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person reading a script through a phone while sitting on a sofa.

quests.instruction: Choose the expression a native speaker would use here.
quests.question: Nobody had prepared, but the speaker was called to give a talk anyway and simply improvised. She decided to ____.
quests.hint: She improvises without preparation.
quests.explanation: To 'wing it' is to do something without preparation, improvising as you go.
quests.usageContext: Informal; common at work and school.
quests.idiomOrigin: From theatre, where actors 'winging it' learned lines quickly in the wings.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture an actor dashing on stage with a script tucked in one hand.

quests.instruction: Pick the most natural idiom for this context.
quests.question: Every time the client asked for the delivery date, the supplier promised to 'look into it' and offered vague excuses, hoping the customer would lose interest. The supplier was ____.
quests.hint: They're being slow on purpose.
quests.explanation: To 'drag your feet' is to delay or act slowly, often because you don't want to do something.
quests.usageContext: Critical; used for bureaucracy, delays and reluctance.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the image of walking slowly and scraping the feet along the ground; recorded in the 20th century.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a child scuffing along the pavement, refusing to go to school.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom that fits best.
quests.question: Nobody wanted to make the hard call about cutting the budget, so the board postponed it again to the next quarter. They were ____.
quests.hint: They keep avoiding a difficult problem by postponing it.
quests.explanation: To 'kick the can down the road' is to postpone dealing with a problem instead of solving it. It suggests that the problem will return.
options: kicking the can down the road
quests.usageContext: Critical; common in politics, economics and management.
quests.idiomOrigin: From the children's game of kicking a can along the street; a modern political phrase.
quests.visualMetaphor: Picture a person nudging a tin can forward on a road, again and again.
